analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and wholesalers import FDA-approved U.S. drugs sold cheaper abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let American pharmacies and wholesalers import FDA-approved drugs sold at lower prices overseas, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in June 1999 and never received a vote or a hearing before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many prescription drugs are approved in the United States and then sold for far less in Canada, Mexico, and Europe. This bill would have amended federal drug law so that drug makers had to keep shipment records, provide proper labeling, and hand those records to American importers — removing the practical barriers that kept U.S. buyers from importing the very same FDA-approved drugs back into the country at foreign prices. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs — especially seniors on fixed incomes and uninsured people — would have had access to the same FDA-approved medicines at the lower prices charged abroad. Pharmacies, wholesalers, and internet pharmacies that import drugs would also gain a legal supply channel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American patients paying U.S. drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required manufacturers of FDA-approved drugs sold in the U.S. and exported — or made abroad for U.S. sale — to keep records for each shipment and provide them on request to qualified U.S. importers, making legal reimportation of the same FDA-approved drugs practical. [S3]

It directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write criteria covering the records, labeling, and the charges manufacturers could impose for providing them, so importers could not be priced or papered out of the market. [S2] [S3]
It covered prescription drugs and insulin, the categories where U.S. vs. foreign price gaps hit consumers hardest. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face competition from their own products sold at lower foreign prices, cutting into the higher U.S. prices that fund their revenue. Health and Human Services would bear the cost of writing and enforcing the new criteria.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs travel a longer supply chain, and critics argued reimportation opened the door to counterfeit or improperly stored medicines reaching American patients — a risk the Food and Drug Administration has long cited. The bill's record-keeping and labeling criteria were designed to address this, but no system eliminates it entirely. [S3]

Manufacturers could plausibly respond by limiting exports or raising foreign prices to protect U.S. pricing, shrinking the savings rather than accepting the competition; the bill's cap on record-service charges was an attempt to limit this but could not force companies to keep selling abroad at low prices. [S3]
Setting up the record and labeling system would impose administrative costs on the manufacturers and on the Department of Health and Human Services. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — lower prices on the same FDA-approved pills for millions of Americans — is large, and the bill targeted only drugs already approved in the U.S., which limits the safety risk compared with broad importation schemes. The main uncertainties are whether manufacturers would game the system by restricting foreign supply, and the administrative burden of policing the supply chain. On balance the savings potential outweighs the manageable risks, but the bill died without anyone testing those risks in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in June 1999; the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on June 9, 1999, joined by Sens. Wellstone, Snowe, and Johnson. [S3] [S5]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day. [S5]
Dorgan made introductory remarks again in January and September 2000, but the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on the bill. [S5]
The bill's only action besides introduction and remarks was the committee referral; no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action appear in its history. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the U.S. market free of cheaper reimported versions of their own drugs and continued charging American patients higher prices than foreigners pay for the same medicines.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered three rounds of introductory remarks over 16 months pressing for action. [S5]

for.name: Sens. Paul Wellstone, Olympia Snowe, and Tim Johnson
for.role: Original cosponsors who introduced the bill with Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Joined Dorgan in introducing the bill on day one. [S3]

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. James Jeffords (R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in June 1999 and never held a markup or reported the bill, keeping it off the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress. [S5]

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug reimportation legislation throughout the late 1990s, arguing it endangered patient safety; the industry's opposition is the standard backdrop for why reimportation bills stalled in committee, though the provided sources do not record its role on this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were bipartisan from the start — five Democrats and one Republican (Sen. Snowe of Maine) among the original cosponsors — but it never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the full Senate would have split. [S3] [S4]

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to supply records and labels enabling U.S. importers to buy their FDA-approved drugs at lower foreign prices, undercutting the higher U.S. prices they charge American patients. Manufacturers would likely have responded by restricting foreign supply or raising foreign prices. [S3]

industries.industry: Pharmacies, wholesalers, and internet pharmacies importing prescription drugs
industries.note: The bill created a legal, documented supply channel for reimportation, letting these businesses sell the same FDA-approved drugs at prices closer to what Canadians or Europeans pay. Consumers who pay their bills are the direct beneficiaries. [S2] [S3]
